title: How Working an Extra 5 Years Impacts Your Retirement Savings
description: The mathematical power of delaying retirement from 62 to 67.
content:
When you are tired of the grind, retiring as soon as possible (often 62) is tempting. However, the financial difference between retiring at 62 and retiring at 67 is not linear; it is exponential. Working 'One More Year' (or five) hits the retirement equation from three sides simultaneously: you save more, your investments grow longer, and your withdrawal period shortens. This 'Triple Threat' can double the safety of your retirement plan. This guide quantifies the value of patience.

Key Takeaways

  • The Social Security Bump: Delaying Social Security from 62 to 67 increases your monthly check by ~30%. Delaying to 70 increases it by ~76%. This is a guaranteed, inflation-protected return.
  • Portfolio Growth: By leaving your $1 Million nest egg untouched for 5 more years, it can grow to $1.4 Million (at 7%) without you adding a penny.
  • Shorter Drawdown: Retiring at 62 means funding 30+ years. Retiring at 67 means funding 25 years. You need a smaller pot of money to cover the shorter duration.
  • Healthcare Bridge: Working until 65 covers you with employer health insurance, saving you $50,000+ in private insurance premiums during the 'Gap Years'.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 'Sequence of Returns' risk is highest early in retirement. By working through a bear market (like 2022) instead of retiring into it, you prevent depleting your portfolio when stocks are down, preserving capital for the long haul.

The 5-Year Comparison

Scenario: You have $500,000 saved at age 62. You earn $80,000.

Option A: Retire Now (62)

  • Portfolio: $500,000.
  • Social Security: Reduced ($1,500/mo).
  • Withdrawal Rate: You need $40k/yr from portfolio (8%).
    Result: High risk of running out of money by age 80.

Option B: Work to 67

  • Contributions: You save $10k/yr for 5 years ($50k).
  • Growth: Your $500k grows to ~$750k (at 7%).
  • Total Portfolio: ~$800,000.
  • Social Security: Full Benefit ($2,200/mo).
  • Withdrawal Rate: You need $25k/yr from portfolio (3%).
    Result: 100% success rate. You die with money.

The Verdict: 5 years of work transformed a 'Failed' retirement into a 'Rich' retirement.

The 'Victory Lap' Compromise

  1. Coast FIRE: You don't have to stay in the high-stress job. Switch to a lower-paying, low-stress job for the 5 years. Cover your bills, but stop saving. Let the portfolio grow.
  2. Part-Time Transition: Ask your employer to go to 3 days a week. You keep benefits (often) and delay drawing down assets, but you get 4-day weekends.
  3. Consulting: Convert your career capital into project work. Earn $50k/year working 6 months. This prevents the portfolio drawdown just as effectively as full-time work.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it worth the stress?

If you are miserable, no. Your health matters. But if you can find a lower-stress way to work, the math is undeniable. It buys financial peace.

What if I die at 68?

That is the risk. You worked 5 extra years for nothing. Balance the math with your health history. If your parents died young, retire earlier.

Does Medicare start at 67?

No, 65. Working until 65 solves the health insurance issue. Working until 67 solves the Social Security issue.
